notes.front: What is a citizen, in one sentence?
notes.back: A person who belongs to a country by birth or by naturalization. The country protects them, and they are loyal to it.
notes.explanation: Several rights and duties on the civics test belong only to citizens, so the idea comes first.
notes.example: Like club membership: gained by birth or by joining, with rights and duties the club sets.
notes.source: Ben's Guide to the U.S. Government, glossary

notes.front: What is the First Amendment, in one sentence?
notes.back: The part of the Bill of Rights listing five freedoms: speech, religion, assembly, the press and petition.
notes.explanation: It is the source of most rights of everyone living in the United States that the test asks about.
notes.example: One amendment bundling five separate freedoms into a single guarantee.

notes.front: What is freedom of speech, in one sentence?
notes.back: The right to say or write what you want without fear of going to jail.
notes.explanation: It is one of the First Amendment's five freedoms, and belongs to everyone living in the US, not only citizens.
notes.example: Publicly criticising a government policy in a newspaper column.

notes.front: What is freedom of religion, in one sentence?
notes.back: The right to practise any religion, or no religion, without government interference.
notes.explanation: It is another First Amendment freedom, and it too belongs to everyone living in the US.
notes.example: Attending any place of worship, or none at all.

notes.front: What is freedom of assembly, in one sentence?
notes.back: The right to gather with other people, for example at a protest or a meeting.
notes.explanation: It is one of the First Amendment's five freedoms.
notes.example: A community holding a peaceful public rally.

notes.front: What is freedom to petition the government, in one sentence?
notes.back: The right to write to the government and ask it to make a change.
notes.explanation: Petitioning means formally asking the government for a change.
notes.example: Example: signing a letter that asks the city to fix a road.

notes.front: What is freedom of expression, as USCIS uses the term?
notes.back: USCIS's own name for a right of everyone living in the United States, alongside freedom of speech.
notes.explanation: M-1778 lists it as a separate accepted answer to question 65, without giving it its own government definition.
notes.example: Example: wearing a T-shirt with a political message.

notes.front: What is the right to bear arms, in one sentence?
notes.back: The Second Amendment right of the people to keep and carry weapons.
notes.explanation: It is in the Second Amendment, not the First, so it is separate from the five First Amendment freedoms.
notes.example: A licensed hunter owning a rifle.
notes.source: The Bill of Rights: A Transcription, Amendment II

notes.front: What is the 15th Amendment, in one sentence?
notes.back: Added in 1870: the right to vote cannot be denied "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude."
notes.explanation: It is the first of four amendments about who can vote.
notes.example: It let a male citizen of any race vote, not only white men.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XV

notes.front: What is the 19th Amendment, in one sentence?
notes.back: Added in 1920: the right to vote cannot be denied "on account of sex."
notes.explanation: It says no citizen can be kept from voting because she is a woman.
notes.example: Example: in 1920, women nationwide won the right to vote in all elections, not only some states.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XIX

notes.front: What is a poll tax, in one sentence?
notes.back: A tax or fee a person had to pay before they were allowed to vote.
notes.explanation: It was one way some states limited voting, before the 24th Amendment banned it in federal elections.
notes.example: A fee charged at the polling place before a ballot was handed over.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XXIV

notes.front: What is the 24th Amendment, in one sentence?
notes.back: Added in 1964: no poll tax can be required to vote in federal elections.
notes.explanation: It removed the poll tax as a barrier to voting for federal office.
notes.example: Example: before 1964, a person could be asked to pay a fee before voting for President or Congress.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XXIV

notes.front: What is the 26th Amendment, in one sentence?
notes.back: Added in 1971: citizens "eighteen years of age or older" cannot be denied the vote because of age.
notes.explanation: It made 18 the voting age in every state.
notes.example: Example: before 1971, some states set the voting age higher than 18.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XXVI

notes.front: What are citizen-only rights, in one sentence?
notes.back: Rights the law reserves to citizens: voting in federal elections, running for federal office and serving on a jury.
notes.explanation: A non-citizen living in the US, even a lawful permanent resident, does not have these three rights.
notes.example: A lawful permanent resident may speak freely but may not vote for President.

notes.front: What is a jury, in one sentence?
notes.back: A group of people who decide whether an accused person is innocent or guilty.
notes.explanation: Serving on a jury is one of the three rights that belong only to citizens.
notes.example: Twelve citizens deciding a criminal trial's verdict.

notes.front: What is the Pledge of Allegiance, in one sentence?
notes.back: The pledge of loyalty "to the Flag of the United States of America, and to the Republic for which it stands."
notes.explanation: Saying it shows loyalty to the flag and to the country.
notes.example: Standing, facing the flag and placing a hand over the heart.
notes.source: 4 USC 4, Pledge of allegiance to the flag

notes.front: What is the Oath of Allegiance, in one sentence?
notes.back: The oath new citizens take: give up other allegiances, support and defend the Constitution, and serve the US if the law requires it.
notes.explanation: Taking it, at a naturalization ceremony, is the moment a person legally becomes a US citizen.
notes.example: Raising a right hand and reciting the oath at a naturalization ceremony.

notes.front: What does it mean to derive citizenship?
notes.back: Becoming a US citizen automatically through a parent, under conditions Congress sets.
notes.explanation: It is one of the three ways in question 68: be born here, naturalize, or derive.
notes.example: Example: a child with a Green Card becomes a citizen when her mother naturalizes.

notes.front: What is the 14th Amendment, in one sentence?
notes.back: Says that all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to its jurisdiction, are citizens.
notes.explanation: It is the constitutional basis for citizenship by birth on US soil.
notes.example: A baby born on US soil is automatically a US citizen.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XIV

notes.front: What is civic participation, in one sentence?
notes.back: Taking part in your community and government, for example voting, joining a political party or writing to a newspaper.
notes.explanation: It is one way citizens and residents act on the freedoms of speech, assembly and petition.
notes.example: Volunteering to help with a political candidate's campaign.

notes.front: What is the federal income tax responsibility, in one sentence?
notes.back: Money everyone living in the US must pay each year to fund the federal government, as the law requires.
notes.explanation: Paying it follows from the rule of law: the law applies to everyone, citizen or not.
notes.example: Sending in a federal tax return by April 15 each year.

notes.front: What is the 16th Amendment, in one sentence?
notes.back: Gives Congress "power to lay and collect taxes on incomes... from whatever source derived."
notes.explanation: It is the constitutional basis for the federal income tax.
notes.example: Before 1913, there was no permanent federal income tax.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XVI

notes.front: What is Selective Service, in one sentence?
notes.back: The registration system that keeps records ready for a possible military draft.
notes.explanation: Registering lets the government call up soldiers fairly if a draft is ever needed.
notes.example: A young man mailing in a Selective Service registration card.

notes.front: What is the draft, as question 72 uses the term?
notes.back: A system of ordering people into military service; USCIS says registering "makes the draft fair, if needed."
notes.explanation: Registration means everyone of the right age is on the list, so a draft is fair.
notes.example: A past war's lottery-style call-up of registered men.

notes.front: There are four amendments to the U.S. Constitution about who can vote. Describe one of them?
notes.back: Citizens eighteen (18) and older can vote.
notes.explanation: This is one of four amendments (15th, 19th, 24th, 26th) about who can vote. Other accepted answers: you don't have to pay a poll tax; any citizen can vote (women and men can vote); a male citizen of any race can vote.

notes.front: One of the four voting amendments concerns age. What does it say?
notes.back: Citizens eighteen (18) and older can vote.
notes.explanation: This is the 26th Amendment (1971), which lowered the voting age to 18.

notes.front: One of the four voting amendments concerns paying to vote. What does it say?
notes.back: You don't have to pay a poll tax to vote.
notes.explanation: This is the 24th Amendment (1964), which banned poll taxes in federal elections.

notes.front: One of the four voting amendments concerns sex. What does it say?
notes.back: Any citizen can vote; women and men can vote.
notes.explanation: This is the 19th Amendment (1920).

notes.front: One of the four voting amendments concerns race. What does it say?
notes.back: A male citizen of any race can vote.
notes.explanation: This is the 15th Amendment (1870), the oldest of the four. Women got the vote later, through the 19th Amendment (1920).

notes.front: Who can vote in federal elections, run for federal office, and serve on a jury in the United States?
notes.back: Citizens.
notes.explanation: Voting in federal elections, running for federal office and serving on a jury are reserved to citizens. Other accepted answers: citizens of the United States; U.S. citizens.

notes.front: What are three rights of everyone living in the United States?
notes.back: Freedom of speech, freedom of religion, freedom of assembly.
notes.explanation: Five of the six accepted answers come from the First Amendment; the sixth, bearing arms, is the Second Amendment. Other accepted answers: freedom of expression; freedom to petition the government; the right to bear arms.

notes.front: Which freedom lets you say or write what you want without fear of jail?
notes.back: Freedom of speech.
notes.explanation: It is one of the six rights of everyone living in the United States (question 65).

notes.front: Which freedom lets you practise any religion, or none?
notes.back: Freedom of religion.
notes.explanation: It is one of the six rights of everyone living in the United States (question 65).

notes.front: Which freedom lets people gather peacefully?
notes.back: Freedom of assembly.
notes.explanation: It is one of the six rights of everyone living in the United States (question 65).

notes.front: Which freedom lets you ask the government for a change?
notes.back: Freedom to petition the government.
notes.explanation: It is one of the six rights of everyone living in the United States (question 65).

notes.front: Besides freedom of speech, what similar freedom does USCIS also list for question 65?
notes.back: Freedom of expression.
notes.explanation: USCIS lists it as a separate accepted answer, close in meaning to freedom of speech.

notes.front: Which of the six question 65 rights comes from the Second Amendment, not the First?
notes.back: The right to bear arms.
notes.explanation: The other five rights of everyone living in the United States all come from the First Amendment.

notes.front: What do we show loyalty to when we say the Pledge of Allegiance?
notes.back: The United States.
notes.explanation: We pledge loyalty to the flag as a symbol of the country itself. Other accepted answer: the flag. (65/20)

notes.front: Name two promises that new citizens make in the Oath of Allegiance?
notes.back: Obey the laws of the United States, and be loyal to the United States.
notes.explanation: The Oath of Allegiance is the legal promise that makes a person a citizen. Other accepted answers: give up loyalty to other countries; defend the (U.S.) Constitution; serve in the military (if needed); serve (help, do important work for) the nation (if needed).

notes.front: One Oath of Allegiance promise concerns other countries. What is it?
notes.back: Give up loyalty to other countries.
notes.explanation: New citizens renounce allegiance to any foreign state as part of the oath.

notes.front: One Oath of Allegiance promise concerns the Constitution. What is it?
notes.back: Defend the (U.S.) Constitution.
notes.explanation: New citizens promise to support and defend the Constitution and laws of the United States.

notes.front: One Oath of Allegiance promise concerns following rules. What is it?
notes.back: Obey the laws of the United States.
notes.explanation: It restates the general responsibility to follow US law.

notes.front: One Oath of Allegiance promise concerns military service. What is it?
notes.back: Serve in the military (if needed).
notes.explanation: New citizens promise to bear arms or perform other required service if the law calls for it.

notes.front: One Oath of Allegiance promise concerns important national work. What is it?
notes.back: Serve (help, do important work for) the nation, if needed.
notes.explanation: It covers non-military service the law might require, such as civilian work of national importance.

notes.front: One Oath of Allegiance promise is a general one. What is it?
notes.back: Be loyal to the United States.
notes.explanation: It sums up the oath's overall promise of allegiance.

notes.front: How can people become United States citizens?
notes.back: Naturalize.
notes.explanation: USCIS lists three ways: be born here, naturalize, or derive citizenship. Other accepted answers: be born in the United States, under the conditions set by the 14th Amendment; derive citizenship (under conditions set by Congress).

notes.front: What are two examples of civic participation in the United States?
notes.back: Vote, and join a political party.
notes.explanation: Civic participation covers many acts beyond voting itself. Other accepted answers: Run for office; Help with a campaign; Join a civic group; Join a community group; Give an elected official your opinion (on an issue); Contact elected officials; Support or oppose an issue or policy; Write to a newspaper.

notes.front: Give one example of civic participation: taking part as a candidate for office?
notes.back: Run for office.
notes.explanation: It is one of USCIS's accepted answers on civic participation (question 69).

notes.front: Give one example of civic participation: joining an organised political group?
notes.back: Join a political party.
notes.explanation: It is one of USCIS's accepted answers on civic participation (question 69).

notes.front: Give one example of civic participation: helping a candidate get elected?
notes.back: Help with a campaign.
notes.explanation: It is one of USCIS's accepted answers on civic participation (question 69).

notes.front: Give one example of civic participation: joining a group focused on public issues?
notes.back: Join a civic group.
notes.explanation: It is one of USCIS's accepted answers on civic participation (question 69).

notes.front: Give one example of civic participation: joining a group focused on your local area?
notes.back: Join a community group.
notes.explanation: It is one of USCIS's accepted answers on civic participation (question 69).

notes.front: Give one example of civic participation: telling an official what you think about an issue?
notes.back: Give an elected official your opinion.
notes.explanation: It is one of USCIS's accepted answers on civic participation (question 69).

notes.front: Give one example of civic participation: reaching out to an official directly?
notes.back: Contact elected officials.
notes.explanation: It is one of USCIS's accepted answers on civic participation (question 69).

notes.front: Give one example of civic participation: publicly taking a side on a policy?
notes.back: Support or oppose an issue or policy.
notes.explanation: It is one of USCIS's accepted answers on civic participation (question 69).

notes.front: Give one example of civic participation: writing about an issue for others to read?
notes.back: Write to a newspaper.
notes.explanation: It is one of USCIS's accepted answers on civic participation (question 69).

notes.front: What is one way Americans can serve their country?
notes.back: Vote.
notes.explanation: Other accepted answers: pay taxes; obey the law; serve in the military; run for office; work for local, state, or federal government.

notes.front: Why is it important to pay federal taxes?
notes.back: Required by law.
notes.explanation: Other accepted answers: all people pay to fund the federal government; required by the 16th Amendment; civic duty.

notes.front: It is important for all men age 18 through 25 to register for the Selective Service. Name one reason why?
notes.back: Required by law.
notes.explanation: Other accepted answers: civic duty; makes the draft fair, if needed.

notes.front: The four amendments that expanded voting rights were ratified in {{c1::1870, 1920, 1964 and 1971}}.
notes.explanation: In order: the 15th (race), the 19th (sex), the 24th (poll tax) and the 26th (age 18).

notes.front: Question 72 says register for Selective Service at "age 18 through 25." What age range does the actual statute give?
notes.back: Between the ages of eighteen and twenty-six (18-26).
notes.explanation: Men must register at 18. The law's range ends at 26.

notes.front: By what date must people usually send in their federal income tax form each year?
notes.back: April 15.
notes.explanation: This is the annual filing deadline the study guide gives for the federal income tax responsibility.

notes.front: The 16th Amendment, which lets Congress tax incomes, was ratified in {{c1::1913}}.
notes.explanation: Before this, there was no permanent constitutional basis for a federal income tax.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XVI

notes.front: The 24th Amendment bans poll taxes in which kind of elections?
notes.back: Federal elections (President, Vice President, senator or representative).
notes.explanation: Its text names elections "for President or Vice President... or for Senator or Representative in Congress."
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XXIV

notes.front: A lawful permanent resident has lived in the US for 10 years. Can they vote in a presidential election without naturalizing?
notes.back: No: voting in federal elections is a citizen-only right.
notes.explanation: Living in the country and holding a green card are not the same as being a citizen.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, any resident can vote
B) No, only citizens can vote in federal elections
C) Only if they pay taxes
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: residence alone is not citizenship. C is wrong: paying taxes is required of everyone, but it does not grant voting rights.

notes.front: A person is arrested only for criticising a government policy in a newspaper column. Does this violate a First Amendment freedom?
notes.back: Yes: it violates freedom of speech and of the press.
notes.explanation: The First Amendment protects criticism of the government as speech, not as a crime.

notes.front: A protester is fined only for saying something the government dislikes, with no threat of violence. Which right protects them?
notes.back: Freedom of speech.
notes.explanation: Speech that merely criticises or disagrees, without threatening harm, is protected.

notes.front: A new immigrant wants to practise a minority religion openly. Does the First Amendment protect this?
notes.back: Yes: freedom of religion covers practising any religion, or none.
notes.explanation: The right belongs to everyone living in the US, not only citizens.

notes.front: A group wants to hold a peaceful public rally about an issue they care about. Which freedom protects them?
notes.back: Freedom of assembly.
notes.explanation: It protects gathering peacefully, distinct from speaking or writing.

notes.front: A resident writes a letter asking their member of Congress to change a law. Which freedom is this?
notes.back: Freedom to petition the government.
notes.explanation: Petitioning means formally asking government for a change, in writing or otherwise.

notes.front: Is the right to keep and bear arms found in the First Amendment or the Second Amendment?
notes.back: The Second Amendment.
notes.explanation: The First Amendment covers speech, religion, assembly and petition; bearing arms is separate.
notes.source: The Bill of Rights: A Transcription, Amendment II

notes.front: In 1870, which amendment let male citizens of any race vote?
notes.back: The 15th Amendment.
notes.explanation: It banned denying the vote because of race, color or previous servitude.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XV

notes.front: Before 1920, a state could refuse to let women vote. Which amendment ended this?
notes.back: The 19th Amendment (1920).
notes.explanation: It banned denying the vote because of sex.
notes.choices:
A) 15th Amendment
B) 19th Amendment
C) 26th Amendment
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the 15th Amendment (1870) addressed race. C is wrong: the 26th Amendment (1971) addressed age, decades later.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XIX

notes.front: Before 1964, some states charged a fee before letting people vote. What was this fee called?
notes.back: A poll tax.
notes.explanation: It was one way states restricted voting before the 24th Amendment banned it in federal elections.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XXIV

notes.front: Which amendment banned poll taxes in federal elections?
notes.back: The 24th Amendment (1964).
notes.explanation: It removed a financial barrier that had kept some citizens from voting.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XXIV

notes.front: A state tries to stop 18-year-olds from voting, saying they are too young. Which amendment makes this illegal?
notes.back: The 26th Amendment (1971).
notes.explanation: It fixed the voting age floor at 18 for the whole country.
notes.choices:
A) 19th Amendment
B) 24th Amendment
C) 26th Amendment
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the 19th Amendment addressed sex, not age. B is wrong: the 24th Amendment addressed poll taxes, not age.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XXVI

notes.front: A green card holder wants to serve on a jury. Is this one of their rights?
notes.back: No: jury service is a citizen-only right.
notes.explanation: Only citizens may vote in federal elections, run for federal office or serve on a jury.

notes.front: Twelve citizens are asked to decide if a defendant is guilty or not guilty. What is this group called?
notes.back: A jury.
notes.explanation: Jury service is one of the three rights and duties that belong only to citizens.

notes.front: During a naturalization ceremony, everyone stands, faces the flag and puts a hand over their heart. What are they saying?
notes.back: The Pledge of Allegiance.
notes.explanation: This is the recitation that shows loyalty to the flag and the country.
notes.source: 4 USC 4, Pledge of allegiance to the flag

notes.front: An applicant raises their right hand at a ceremony and promises to "support and defend the Constitution." What is happening?
notes.back: They are taking the Oath of Allegiance and becoming a citizen.
notes.explanation: The oath, not the Pledge, is the legal step that completes naturalization.
notes.choices:
A) Reciting the Pledge of Allegiance
B) Taking the Oath of Allegiance
C) Registering for Selective Service
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the Pledge does not mention defending the Constitution or make someone a citizen. C is wrong: Selective Service registration is unrelated to naturalization.

notes.front: A baby is born in the United States to two non-citizen parents. Under the 14th Amendment, is the baby a US citizen?
notes.back: Yes, if subject to US jurisdiction, as the Amendment provides.
notes.explanation: The 14th Amendment grants citizenship by birth on US soil, not by a parent's citizenship.
notes.source: Amendments 11-27 to the Constitution, Amendment XIV

notes.front: A citizen who has never voted instead joins a local civic group to work on an issue. Does this count as civic participation?
notes.back: Yes: civic participation includes acts other than voting.
notes.explanation: Joining a civic or community group is one of USCIS's own listed examples.

notes.front: Every April, a worker sends a form to the government reporting their income. What responsibility is this?
notes.back: Paying federal income tax.
notes.explanation: It is required by law of everyone living in the United States.

notes.front: A male US citizen turns 18. What is he required by law to do regarding Selective Service?
notes.back: Register with the Selective Service System.
notes.explanation: The law requires registration from age 18 up to 26.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing until drafted
B) Register with Selective Service
C) Enlist in the military
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: registration is required now, not only if a draft happens. C is wrong: registering is not the same as enlisting.

notes.front: What is the difference between the Pledge of Allegiance and the Oath of Allegiance?
notes.back: The Pledge shows loyalty to the flag and country; the Oath is the legal promise that makes someone a citizen.
notes.explanation: Both express loyalty, but only the Oath has legal effect: taking it completes naturalization.
notes.contrast: The Pledge is words of loyalty. The Oath is the promise that makes you a citizen.

notes.front: What is the difference between rights of everyone living in the US and citizen-only rights?
notes.back: Everyone: speech, religion, assembly, petition, bearing arms. Citizens only: vote for President and Congress, run for federal office, serve on a jury.
notes.explanation: The First and Second Amendment freedoms apply to all residents; political participation rights apply only to citizens.
notes.contrast: Citizens only: vote for President and Congress, run for federal office, serve on a jury.
